intro: Raudonė, a village on the Nemunas beside a 16th-century castle, holds a seven-trunked lime in the castle park, voted Lithuania's Tree of the Year 2018. Local legend says it split into seven trunks after seven serfs were chained and whipped to death against it. Two more oaks widen the outing: the Plokščiai Oak, newly protected and once hollow enough for children to climb inside, across the Nemunas; and the Ilguva Oak, a longer detour off any marked path, put at 300 to 400 years by the state register.
meta_description: The Raudonė Castle Lime, Lithuania's Tree of the Year 2018, plus two nearby oaks within Panemunių Regional Park across the Nemunas.
question_meta: Raudonė's oldest confirmed tree is the Castle Lime, a seven-trunked lime roughly 400 years old, Tree of the Year 2018. Full list of 3.
question_answer: The Raudonė Castle Lime, a small-leaved lime with seven trunks growing in the park of Raudonė Castle, estimated at about 400 years old by the state register. Two further oaks within Panemunių Regional Park, across the Nemunas, are day-trip additions rather than closer rivals for the title.
question_context:
In 2018 the Lithuanian Arboriculture Centre named this lime the country's Tree of the Year, and it went on to represent Lithuania in the European Tree of the Year 2019 contest. Its seven trunks spread into an egg-shaped canopy 20 metres tall and 19 wide, covering some 220 square metres of the castle park. A metal rod is embedded between two trunks about three metres up, and local legend says seven serfs were once chained to it and whipped to death, and that the tree split into seven trunks from the horror of it. The state register puts its actual age at roughly 400 years. The castle now houses a primary school, but the park and tower are an established, ticketed attraction, so the tree is reachable despite the school on site.

Two oaks widen the visit into Panemunių Regional Park proper. The Plokščiai Oak stands 2.8 kilometres away on the opposite bank, beside a war memorial, once hollow enough for children to climb inside, 34 metres tall. The Ilguva Oak is a longer detour, 12.7 kilometres out, off any marked path and dated at 300 to 400 years, the oldest confirmed age here.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Raudonė?
faq.a: The Raudonė Castle Lime, a seven-trunked lime estimated at roughly 400 years old, in the park of Raudonė Castle.

faq.q: Why does the tree have seven trunks?
faq.a: Nobody knows for certain. A local legend, told as folklore rather than fact by the regional park itself, links the split to a story of seven serfs whipped to death against the trunk.
The castle park is free to walk; the castle tower itself is a ticketed attraction. The two nearby oaks are free too, on open forest and roadside land.

faq.q: Has this tree won any awards?
faq.a: Yes. It was voted Lithuania's Tree of the Year in 2018 and went on to the European Tree of the Year 2019 contest.

faq.q: Are there other old trees near Raudonė?
faq.a: Yes, two, both within Panemunių Regional Park across the Nemunas: the Plokščiai Oak, 2.8km away and hollow enough for children to once climb inside it, and the Ilguva Oak, a 12.7km detour off any marked path, put at 300 to 400 years by the state register.

trees.story:
Seven trunks, and a legend that accounts for them in the worst way available. A metal rod sits embedded between two of the stems about three metres up, and local tradition holds that seven serfs were once chained to that rod and whipped to death, and that the lime split into seven from the horror of it. The Panemunė Regional Park repeats the story on its own pages as folklore rather than as record, which is exactly how to take it.

Strip the legend away and the tree still earns the drive. The state register puts it at about 400 years old. It measures 6.2 metres round at chest height and 31 metres tall, under an egg-shaped crown 20 metres deep and 19 across that shades some 220 square metres of ground. In 2018 the Lithuanian Arboriculture Centre named it Lithuania's Tree of the Year, on a nomination from the regional park, and in 2019 it went forward to the European Tree of the Year contest.

It stands about forty metres east of Raudonė Castle, beside a Soviet-era memorial to the Second World War. The castle itself is a primary school now, with a tower open to visitors for around a euro and a half; the park where the lime grows costs nothing and needs no ticket. The Nemunas runs below, and the regional park along with it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its seven trunks and the metal rod embedded between two of them about 3 metres up, 6.2 metres round. It stands beside a Soviet era war memorial, 40 metres east of Raudone Castle.

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.name: The Plokščiai Oak (Panemunė)

location.address: Beside the 'Kentėjimo kelias' (Suffering Path) memorial, near road 3807 (Kiduliai-Gelgaudiškis-Gerdžiūnai), Plokščiai village, on the south bank of the Nemunas within Panemunių Regional Park, Šakiai district

trees.story:
Children in Plokščiai used to climb inside this oak. The base of the trunk rotted out long ago, leaving a hollow big enough to play in, and people who grew up in the village still remember doing it.

The hollow has not stopped it growing. It stands 34 metres tall, which is a great deal for an oak. The trunk is 5.2 metres round.

For all that, it had no official status until very recently. Lithuania's Environment Ministry designated it only in September 2025, in the same order that protected a wave of other big oaks across the country, including the Netoniai oak outside Kaunas. It is one of the eleven natural heritage objects of Panemunių Regional Park, the stretch of the Nemunas valley famous for its castles.

It grows on the south bank of the river, beside the Kentėjimo kelias, the Suffering Path memorial, near the road through Plokščiai village. That puts it about 2.8 kilometres by road from the Castle Lime at Raudonė on the far side of the valley, close enough to make the two a single outing. There is another Plokščiai oak in Kretinga district, near Klaipėda; this is not it.

Nobody has published an age for this tree. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.access: Free; stands on public land within Panemunių Regional Park, beside a public road and a memorial site
trees.transport: Šakiai district, about 2.8km from Raudonė (Jurbarkas district) by road, on the opposite side of the Nemunas within the same regional park; reachable by car, no public transit checked this pass
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its great height, 34 metres, above a trunk 5.2 metres round and hollow at the base. It stands beside the Kentėjimo kelias memorial by the road through Plokščiai, across the Nemunas from Raudonė.

trees.name: Ilguva Oak

location.address: About 130m south of Ilguva Church, within the Nykos landscape reserve, Ilguva village, Kriūkai eldership, Šakiai district

trees.story:
This is the oak you have to look for. It stands off any marked path on a slope in the Nykos landscape reserve, and the usual way in is on foot along the Nyka stream from the village of Dulinčiškiai, then up the bank. The pin gets you close; the last stretch is yours.

What you find is worth the scramble. The trunk is 5.42 metres round at chest height, measured in 2014, and at 3.8 metres it splits into three stems that carry the tree to 32 metres. The crown alone is 22 metres tall and 22 metres wide, as broad as it is deep.

The state cadastre puts it at 300 to 400 years old. That range is the register's own, not something we worked out, and it has been protected since 2005. Even the low end means this oak was already growing on its slope when the Nemunas valley below was still part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

It is 12.7 kilometres from Raudonė by road, a longer detour than the Plokščiai oak across the river, and best treated as a small expedition of its own; Ilguva's church, about 130 metres to the north, is the landmark to aim for. Everything here rests on one published source, the cadastre as Lithuanian Wikipedia reports it. If you find the tree, a photograph and a word about the way in would help the next person.
trees.access: Free, but genuinely hard to find: no gate or ownership restriction, but the tree stands off any marked path, reached by walking along the Nyka stream from Dulinčiškiai village (in Panemunė) and climbing a slope
trees.transport: Šakiai district; about 12.7km from Raudonė by road, no public transit checked this pass
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.42 metres round, splitting into three stems at 3.8 metres under a crown 22 metres wide. It stands off the paths on a slope above the Nyka stream, about 130 metres south of Ilguva Church.
